subtopic_detail: Sequencing trauma focused therapy alongside alcohol dependence
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 38 year old woman with nightmares, flashbacks and hypervigilance since a violent assault four years ago. She avoids the suburb where it happened and has not travelled on public transport since.

She drinks about twelve standard drinks daily, starting mid morning, and describes shaking hands and sweating until the first drink. She has never had a withdrawal seizure or delirium. She has read about eye movement therapy and asks to start it, and says a previous service told her she had to be dry for six months before they would see her. She has no psychotic symptoms and no current suicidal intent, and her liver function shows a mildly raised gamma glutamyl transferase with normal synthetic function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands, no asterixis, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Gamma glutamyl transferase 180 U/L (5-50); albumin, bilirubin and international normalised ratio within normal limits; full blood count shows mean cell volume 101 fL (80-100)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Require six months of abstinence before starting any trauma therapy
options.rationale: Mandatory abstinence periods exclude the patients most in need and are not supported by Australian guidance, which recommends integrated rather than sequential care (Source: Phoenix Australia Guidelines for PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Guidelines for PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.text: Start sertraline alone and defer any trauma focused therapy for now
options.rationale: Medication is an adjunct in this disorder and trauma focused psychological therapy is the first line treatment, so relying on an antidepressant alone withholds the intervention with the largest effect (Source: Phoenix Australia Guidelines for PTSD and Complex PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Guidelines for PTSD and Complex PTSD

options.text: Offer withdrawal management and trauma focused therapy together
options.rationale: Physical dependence with morning tremor and sweating needs medically supervised withdrawal with thiamine and a benzodiazepine regimen, and trauma focused therapy is then delivered concurrently rather than held back until an abstinence milestone (Source: Phoenix Australia Guidelines for PTSD and Complex PTSD; Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Guidelines for PTSD and Complex PTSD
Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

options.text: Begin eye movement therapy without addressing her daily drinking
options.rationale: Proceeding without withdrawal management risks unplanned withdrawal during therapy and alcohol will continue to be used to blunt the distress that exposure work deliberately raises (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

options.text: Refer to residential rehabilitation and review her in twelve months
options.rationale: Residential programmes suit people with unstable housing or repeated community treatment failure, and a twelve month review leaves a treatable disorder unaddressed in the meantime (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems).
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

explanation.summary: Alcohol use disorder co occurs with post traumatic stress disorder in a large proportion of cases, most often because alcohol is used to suppress intrusions and hyperarousal. Traditional practice sequenced treatment by demanding abstinence first, but this excludes the people with the most severe illness and the evidence now supports integrated concurrent care. Physical dependence still needs to be managed, because unplanned withdrawal during exposure work is both dangerous and destabilising, so supervised withdrawal with thiamine and a tapering benzodiazepine regimen comes first in sequence but not months in advance. Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing have comparable evidence, and the choice is made with the patient rather than by protocol.
key_points: Post traumatic stress disorder and alcohol use disorder are treated concurrently, not sequentially
Mandatory abstinence periods exclude the most severely affected patients
Morning tremor and sweating indicate physical dependence needing supervised withdrawal
Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line and medication is adjunctive
Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement therapy have comparable evidence
explanation.pearls: Give parenteral thiamine before any carbohydrate load in a dependent drinker, because glucose given first can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a thiamine deplete brain within hours.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Guidelines for PTSD and Complex PTSD
Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

subtopic_detail: Medical instability threshold before outpatient family based treatment
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 15 year old girl brought by her parents, who have read about a family based approach and want to start it at home this week. Over eight months she has cut out whole food groups, runs before school and has lost 14 kg.

She says she feels cold all the time and fainted once last week getting out of the shower. Her periods stopped four months ago. Her weight is 41 kg for a height of 165 cm and her parents are engaged, capable and have taken leave from work to supervise meals. She has no suicidal thoughts and no self harm, and her electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a normal corrected QT interval.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38 while awake, blood pressure 88/54 lying and 66/40 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 35.4
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 15.1 kg/m2, cool peripheries with lanugo hair, unable to rise from squatting without using her arms
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); phosphate 0.8 mmol/L (0.75-1.5); glucose 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for medical stabilisation before starting family based treatment
options.rationale: A waking pulse of 38, a postural blood pressure drop of that size, a temperature of 35.4 and hypoglycaemia each independently meet Australian criteria for admission, and refeeding must occur with monitoring before outpatient therapy can begin (Source: ANZAED Practice Guidelines; RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

options.text: Start outpatient family based treatment with weekly weighing for her
options.rationale: Family based treatment is the correct outpatient therapy for adolescent anorexia nervosa, but it presumes medical stability and cannot be delivered safely to a bradycardic hypoglycaemic patient (Source: ANZAED Practice Guidelines).

options.text: Refer for individual cognitive behavioural therapy for her eating disorder
options.rationale: Individual therapy has weaker evidence than family based treatment in this age group and, like any outpatient option, does not address the immediate physiological risk (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

options.text: Start olanzapine at a low dose to assist with her weight restoration
options.rationale: Olanzapine produces modest weight gain and can reduce anxiety around eating, but it is adjunctive and is not a substitute for supervised refeeding in an unstable patient (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

options.text: Arrange dietitian review and repeat the observations in a week for her
options.rationale: Deferring by a week in the presence of bradycardia and hypoglycaemia accepts a real risk of sudden cardiac death, which is the leading cause of mortality in this condition (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

explanation.summary: Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric illness, and the deaths are from cardiac events, hypoglycaemia and suicide rather than from starvation alone. Australian admission criteria are explicitly physiological and include a heart rate below about 50 while awake, a postural drop of more than 20 mmHg systolic, a temperature below 35.5, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, a prolonged corrected QT interval and rapid weight loss. Family based treatment is the evidence based outpatient therapy for adolescents and works by returning control of refeeding to capable parents, but it starts only once the patient is medically stable. Refeeding syndrome is the hazard of the first week, so phosphate, magnesium and potassium are measured daily during initial refeeding with thiamine cover.
key_points: Admission criteria in anorexia nervosa are physiological and objective
A waking heart rate below about 50 or a systolic postural drop over 20 mmHg triggers admission
Family based treatment is first line for adolescents once medically stable
Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia signal exhausted reserve and imminent risk
Monitor phosphate, magnesium and potassium daily during early refeeding
explanation.pearls: A falling serum phosphate in the first week of refeeding is the earliest marker of refeeding syndrome and appears before any clinical change, so it is replaced actively rather than watched while feeding continues.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

subtopic_detail: Sequence of investigation for a thyroid nodule with suppressed thyrotropin
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 48 year old woman who had a carotid ultrasound arranged after a transient episode of dizziness, and the report incidentally describes a 2.5 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe with smooth margins and no microcalcification.

She has noticed no lump herself and has no difficulty swallowing, no voice change and no neck pain. She had no radiation exposure in childhood and no family history of thyroid cancer or endocrine tumours. She mentions she has felt warmer than others recently and her resting heart rate has been higher on her fitness watch. Her thyroid function has come back today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Smooth mobile 2.5 cm right thyroid nodule, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no proptosis or lid lag
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 0.08 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); free thyroxine 19.4 pmol/L (10-20); ultrasound shows a 2.5 cm solid isoechoic nodule with smooth margins and no microcalcification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Perform ultrasound guided fine needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule
options.rationale: Aspiration is the correct next test when thyrotropin is normal or raised, but an autonomously functioning nodule commonly yields cytology suspicious for follicular neoplasm and leads to unnecessary surgery (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance

options.text: Arrange thyroid scintigraphy before considering any biopsy of the nodule
options.rationale: A suppressed thyrotropin raises the possibility of an autonomously functioning nodule, and a hot nodule on radionuclide scanning is almost never malignant so it is treated rather than biopsied (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance

options.text: Measure thyroglobulin and calcitonin to stratify her risk of malignancy
options.rationale: Thyroglobulin is a surveillance marker after treatment of differentiated cancer rather than a diagnostic test, and calcitonin screening for medullary carcinoma is not routine in Australian practice (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance

options.text: Repeat the neck ultrasound in twelve months without any biopsy now
options.rationale: Interval surveillance suits small sonographically benign nodules with normal thyroid function, and it ignores the biochemical abnormality that needs explanation (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance

options.text: Refer for hemithyroidectomy given the size of the nodule on imaging
options.rationale: Size alone does not determine surgery, and operating before establishing function or cytology exposes her to hypothyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve risk without indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Thyroid nodules are found in a large proportion of adults imaged for other reasons, and the entire diagnostic pathway begins with a thyroid stimulating hormone measurement rather than with a needle. A suppressed level shifts the pathway to radionuclide scanning, because a nodule that concentrates tracer is autonomously functioning and carries a negligible risk of malignancy. Cold or indeterminate nodules and those with a normal or raised thyrotropin proceed to ultrasound risk stratification and fine needle aspiration according to size and sonographic features. Treating a toxic nodule with radioiodine or surgery addresses both the biochemistry and the nodule, whereas biopsying it generates a follicular result that cannot distinguish adenoma from carcinoma on cytology.
key_points: Thyroid stimulating hormone is the first test for any thyroid nodule
A suppressed level directs the pathway to scintigraphy rather than biopsy
Hot nodules are almost never malignant and are treated rather than sampled
Cold nodules are risk stratified on ultrasound and sampled by size and features
Cytology cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma
explanation.pearls: Radioiodine is the usual definitive treatment for a toxic autonomous nodule in Australia, and thyroid function is rechecked at six to eight weeks because hypothyroidism after treatment is far less common than with radioiodine given for Graves disease.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Thyroid Nodule Guidance

subtopic_detail: Second line eradication after failed first line therapy for Helicobacter pylori
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45 year old man with eight months of epigastric burning that wakes him at night. A urea breath test six months ago was positive and you prescribed esomeprazole with amoxicillin and clarithromycin for seven days.

He brought the empty packets to his review and confirms he took every dose. He stopped the proton pump inhibitor two weeks before the follow up breath test and had taken no antibiotics in that period. That repeat breath test, done six weeks after finishing treatment, is again positive. He has no dysphagia, no vomiting, no weight loss and no anaemia, and he has no allergy to penicillin.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Repeat urea breath test positive six weeks after completing therapy; haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180); iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the same triple therapy for a further fourteen days of treatment
options.rationale: Failure of a clarithromycin containing regimen in an adherent patient indicates macrolide resistance, and repeating the same combination for longer selects further resistance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy with biopsy for culture before any further therapy
options.rationale: Endoscopic culture and susceptibility testing is reserved for failure after two or more empirical regimens, or where alarm features demand endoscopy in its own right (Source: GESA clinical guidance on Helicobacter pylori).
source_refs: GESA clinical guidance on Helicobacter pylori

options.text: Give a proton pump inhibitor alone and retest him again in three months
options.rationale: Acid suppression relieves symptoms but does not eradicate the organism, and it suppresses bacterial load enough to cause false negative breath testing (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Give a levofloxacin based triple regimen for seven days starting now
options.rationale: A quinolone based regimen is a recognised salvage option but sits behind bismuth quadruple therapy in Australian sequencing because of resistance rates and tendon and neurological adverse effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Give a bismuth based quadruple regimen for fourteen days starting now
options.rationale: Bismuth subcitrate with a proton pump inhibitor, tetracycline and metronidazole for fourteen days is the recommended second line regimen because it avoids clarithromycin entirely and achieves high eradication rates after macrolide failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal; GESA clinical guidance on Helicobacter pylori).
source_refs: GESA clinical guidance on Helicobacter pylori

explanation.summary: Helicobacter pylori eradication rates with standard clarithromycin triple therapy have fallen worldwide as macrolide resistance has risen, and confirmed failure in an adherent patient should be assumed to reflect resistance rather than non compliance. Second line therapy follows the principle of not reusing clarithromycin, so bismuth quadruple therapy for fourteen days is the standard Australian choice. Testing of cure is essential and must be performed at least four weeks after antibiotics and two weeks after stopping acid suppression, since both suppress the organism and generate false negatives. Persistent failure after two regimens is the point at which endoscopy with culture and susceptibility testing becomes worthwhile, alongside consideration of alternative causes for the symptoms.
key_points: Failure of clarithromycin triple therapy in an adherent patient implies macrolide resistance
Never reuse clarithromycin in a second line regimen
Bismuth quadruple therapy for fourteen days is the standard second line option
Test of cure requires four weeks off antibiotics and two weeks off acid suppression
Endoscopic culture and susceptibility testing follows two failed empirical regimens
explanation.pearls: Warn patients that bismuth turns the tongue and stools black, because unwarned patients frequently stop the course believing they have gastrointestinal bleeding and the regimen then fails on adherence rather than resistance.

sources.label: GESA clinical guidance on Helicobacter pylori

subtopic_detail: Disposition after computed tomography confirms a distal ureteric stone
stem:
You are the emergency department resident caring for a 41 year old man who arrived four hours ago with sudden severe right sided back pain that came in waves and made him unable to sit still. He has vomited twice and says his urine looked pink this morning.

His pain settled well after intravenous ketorolac and he is now comfortable and eating. He has no fever, no rigors and no dysuria. His urinalysis shows blood without nitrites or leucocytes, and his creatinine is normal. Computed tomography of the kidneys, ureters and bladder shows a 4 mm calculus at the right vesicoureteric junction with mild proximal hydronephrosis and no perinephric stranding, and both kidneys are of normal size.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 132/80, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness only, abdomen soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110); white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); urinalysis shows blood without nitrites or leucocytes; computed tomography shows a 4 mm right vesicoureteric junction calculus with mild hydronephrosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit him for intravenous fluids to help flush the stone through
options.rationale: Forced diuresis does not increase stone passage rates and increases pain by raising pressure proximal to the obstruction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology; RACGP guidance on renal colic).

options.text: Arrange urgent ureteric stenting by the urology registrar on call today
options.rationale: Emergency decompression is indicated for infection above an obstruction, acute kidney injury, a solitary kidney or intractable pain, and none of those features is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology).

options.text: Book extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy for him within 24 hours
options.rationale: Lithotripsy is considered for larger or proximal stones that fail to pass, and a 4 mm distal stone has a high spontaneous passage rate that makes intervention unnecessary (Source: RACGP guidance on renal colic).

options.text: Discharge with analgesia and tamsulosin with urology review arranged
options.rationale: Stones under 5 mm pass spontaneously in around 80 per cent of cases, so oral analgesia with an alpha blocker for a distal stone plus outpatient follow up and clear return advice is appropriate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology; RACGP guidance on renal colic).

options.text: Start empirical oral antibiotics and repeat the imaging in a week
options.rationale: There is no fever, no pyuria and no nitrites, so antibiotics treat nothing and repeat computed tomography adds radiation without changing management (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Non contrast computed tomography is the reference standard for renal colic in Australia and answers the three questions that determine management, namely stone size, stone position and whether there is obstruction or infection. Spontaneous passage is strongly size dependent, with around 80 per cent of stones under 5 mm passing and fewer than 20 per cent of those above 8 mm doing so. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs outperform opioids for this pain because they reduce ureteric wall oedema and renal capsular pressure as well as providing analgesia. The single dangerous scenario is an infected obstructed system, which requires immediate decompression by stent or nephrostomy alongside antibiotics, because antibiotics alone cannot sterilise an obstructed collecting system.
key_points: Stones under 5 mm pass spontaneously in around 80 per cent of cases
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are the analgesia of choice
Alpha blockers assist passage of distal ureteric stones
Fever with obstruction demands urgent decompression, not antibiotics alone
Urgent intervention is also indicated for acute kidney injury or a solitary kidney
explanation.pearls: Send every passed stone for analysis and arrange a metabolic screen after a second episode, because uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain films and can be dissolved with urinary alkalinisation rather than removed surgically.

subtopic_detail: Synpharyngitic haematuria with normal complement in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old man who noticed his urine turned the colour of cola yesterday morning. He developed a sore throat the day before that and still has one.

He has had two similar episodes over the past three years, each lasting a couple of days and each starting within a day of a cold, and on both occasions he was told it was a urinary infection although no organism was ever grown. He has no rash, no joint swelling and no abdominal pain. His urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, and his complement C3 and C4 levels are both within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Pharyngeal erythema without exudate, no rash, no oedema, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); urine protein creatinine ratio 60 mg/mmol (less than 30); urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat him with penicillin and repeat the urine test in six weeks time
options.rationale: This is the pathway for post streptococcal disease, which follows the infection by one to three weeks and depresses C3, whereas his haematuria began within a day and his complement is normal (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography urography to find a bleeding source now
options.rationale: Urological imaging is directed at non glomerular bleeding from tumour or stone, and dysmorphic cells with red cell casts localise the bleeding to the glomerulus (Source: RACGP guidance on haematuria).

options.text: Refer to nephrology for consideration of a renal biopsy for him
options.rationale: Recurrent visible haematuria beginning within a day of a mucosal infection, with red cell casts, proteinuria and normal complement, indicates a glomerulonephritis needing histological diagnosis and blood pressure management (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis; RACGP guidance on haematuria).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone now and review the proteinuria later
options.rationale: Immunosuppression is reserved for defined histological patterns with persistent proteinuria despite blockade of the renin angiotensin system, and giving it before biopsy commits him to treatment without a diagnosis (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Reassure him that this is benign haematuria and no action is needed
options.rationale: Proteinuria above 50 mg/mmol with a rising blood pressure marks progressive disease rather than a benign course, and it identifies exactly the patients who need surveillance (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis).

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and classically produces visible haematuria within 24 to 48 hours of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection, which is why it is called synpharyngitic. That timing is the key discriminator from post streptococcal glomerulonephritis, where the latency is one to three weeks and complement C3 falls. Prognosis is determined by proteinuria, blood pressure and the degree of fibrosis on biopsy rather than by the visible haematuria itself, and a substantial minority progress to kidney failure over decades. Treatment centres on blood pressure control to a low target with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker, with immunosuppression reserved for persistent significant proteinuria.
key_points: Synpharyngitic haematuria appears within 24 to 48 hours of the infection
Post streptococcal disease follows after one to three weeks and depresses C3
Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Prognosis is driven by proteinuria, blood pressure and fibrosis rather than haematuria
First line therapy is renin angiotensin blockade with a low blood pressure target
explanation.pearls: Visible haematuria within a day of a sore throat with a normal C3 points to immunoglobulin A nephropathy, whereas a one to three week gap with a low C3 that recovers by eight weeks defines post streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

subtopic_detail: Crystals in synovial fluid do not exclude coexisting septic arthritis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman admitted overnight with a hot swollen right knee that became painful over two days. She has osteoarthritis and hypertension, has never had a joint replacement and has had one similar episode in the same knee three years ago that settled with tablets.

She has been shivery at home and her family say she has been more confused than usual. The knee is warm with a moderate effusion and she resists any movement. You have aspirated the joint and the fluid is turbid yellow. Polarised light microscopy shows positively birefringent rhomboid crystals and the Gram stain shows no organisms, with culture pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 124/70, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen right knee with moderate effusion, resists all passive movement, no overlying break in the skin
data_table.Investigations: Synovial white cell count 42 x10^9/L with 88 per cent neutrophils; positively birefringent rhomboid crystals present; synovial Gram stain negative with culture pending; blood white cell count 13.5 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 140 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start oral colchicine and review the knee again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Colchicine treats the crystal component but leaves a possible joint infection untreated, and 48 hours is long enough for cartilage destruction to become irreversible (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics while awaiting the synovial fluid culture
options.rationale: Crystals and infection coexist often enough that identifying crystals never excludes sepsis, and a synovial count above 50 x10^9/L is not required when fever, systemic upset and inflammatory markers point to infection, so empirical flucloxacillin starts after cultures are taken (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Rheumatology Association guidance).

options.text: Give an intra articular corticosteroid injection into the affected knee
options.rationale: Injecting steroid into a potentially infected joint accelerates bacterial proliferation and is contraindicated until infection has been excluded by culture (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association guidance).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for five days and review her then
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid is a reasonable treatment for crystal arthritis in an older patient with renal impairment, but it suppresses the response to an untreated infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Start regular naproxen with proton pump inhibitor cover for her now
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs carry substantial renal and gastrointestinal risk at this age and, like the other options, treat only the crystal component (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Septic arthritis destroys articular cartilage within days and carries a mortality of around ten per cent, so the diagnostic approach is deliberately biased toward treating uncertainty rather than excluding it. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are positively birefringent and rhomboid, distinguishing them from the negatively birefringent needles of urate, but neither finding rules out coexisting infection since crystals are frequently present in the joints of older adults. The synovial white cell count is a continuum rather than a threshold, and Gram stain is negative in roughly half of culture proven septic arthritis. Management is joint aspiration for culture, empirical intravenous antibiotics and orthopaedic review for washout, with de escalation once cultures return.
key_points: Crystals in synovial fluid never exclude coexisting septic arthritis
Positively birefringent rhomboid crystals indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition
Gram stain is negative in about half of culture proven septic arthritis
Aspirate for culture before the first antibiotic dose
Intra articular and systemic corticosteroids are withheld until infection is excluded
explanation.pearls: Chondrocalcinosis on a knee radiograph confirms calcium pyrophosphate deposition but has no bearing on whether that joint is currently infected, and finding it should never be used to stand down antibiotics in a febrile patient.

subtopic_detail: Drug induced acute interstitial nephritis in a euvolaemic patient
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68 year old man whose routine bloods show a creatinine that has climbed from 78 micromol/L six months ago to 236 micromol/L today. He feels reasonably well and has noticed only some tiredness.

He has taken ramipril for five years at an unchanged dose and started pantoprazole eight weeks ago for reflux. He has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, drinks normally and his weight is unchanged. He has no rash, no joint pain and no fever. He is euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no postural drop, and his renal ultrasound reports normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and no asymmetry.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 132/78 with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no rash, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 236 micromol/L (60-110) risen from 78 six months ago; urine protein creatinine ratio 40 mg/mmol (less than 30); urine microscopy shows white cells and white cell casts with no growth on culture; eosinophils 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); renal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the ramipril and recheck his creatinine again in one week
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors cause a rise in creatinine when renal perfusion falls or after a dose change, and his dose has been unchanged for five years with no volume depletion (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Give a two litre intravenous fluid challenge to him over four hours
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation is the correct response to a pre renal picture, and he is euvolaemic with no postural drop and a sterile pyuria that points elsewhere (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Start oral prednisolone before any of his medications are stopped
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered when function fails to recover after the drug is withdrawn and the diagnosis is confirmed histologically, so giving them while the culprit continues is illogical (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Refer him for urgent haemodialysis given the level of his creatinine
options.rationale: Dialysis is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload, uraemic complications or certain poisonings, and a creatinine value alone never establishes the need (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Stop the proton pump inhibitor and monitor his renal function closely
options.rationale: Sterile pyuria with white cell casts, modest proteinuria and peripheral eosinophilia in a euvolaemic patient describes acute interstitial nephritis, and proton pump inhibitors are now a leading cause, so withdrawal of the drug is both the treatment and the diagnostic test (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

explanation.summary: Acute interstitial nephritis is an immune mediated reaction of the renal interstitium to a drug, and proton pump inhibitors have overtaken antibiotics as the most frequently implicated class in older populations. The classical triad of fever, rash and eosinophilia is present in fewer than ten per cent of cases, so its absence carries no weight and the diagnosis rests on the pattern of sterile pyuria, white cell casts and sub nephrotic proteinuria in a patient who is not volume depleted. The latency from starting the drug is typically weeks to months, which is longer than for most other drug reactions and often means the drug is overlooked. Recovery is usually good if the agent is withdrawn early, whereas prolonged exposure leads to interstitial fibrosis and permanent impairment.
key_points: Proton pump inhibitors are now a leading cause of drug induced interstitial nephritis
The classical triad of fever, rash and eosinophilia occurs in under ten per cent
Sterile pyuria with white cell casts is the characteristic urinary finding
Latency from starting the drug is typically weeks to months
Withdrawal of the culprit drug is both the treatment and the diagnostic test
explanation.pearls: If creatinine has not improved within about a week of stopping the drug, refer for biopsy rather than continuing to observe, because corticosteroids started within two weeks of onset give the best chance of full functional recovery.

sources.label: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

subtopic_detail: Pancytopenia with macrocytosis and a low reticulocyte count
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66 year old man referred with three months of fatigue and bruises appearing on his shins and forearms without injury. He has needed to stop halfway up his driveway to catch his breath.

He drinks two beers a week, takes no regular medication and has had no recent infection or travel. He has no lymphadenopathy and no splenomegaly, and there is no jaundice. His blood film is reported as showing occasional hypogranular neutrophils with no blasts seen. His vitamin B12, folate, thyroid function and liver function are all within normal limits, and his reticulocyte count is low.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 128/74, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Pallor of the conjunctivae, scattered ecchymoses over the shins and forearms, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180); mean cell volume 106 fL (80-100); platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400); neutrophils 1.1 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); reticulocytes 12 x10^9/L (20-100); vitamin B12, folate, thyroid and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin and repeat the count in a month
options.rationale: A normal vitamin B12 with normal folate excludes megaloblastic anaemia as the explanation for the macrocytosis, and empirical replacement would delay the diagnosis by a month (Source: Cancer Council Australia haematology guidance).

options.text: Transfuse red cells and platelets and review him in the outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Transfusion is supportive rather than diagnostic and he is neither symptomatically anaemic at rest nor bleeding actively, so it would not establish the cause (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Start prednisolone for presumed immune mediated platelet destruction
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia is an isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal or raised reticulocyte response, and does not explain the accompanying anaemia and neutropenia (Source: Cancer Council Australia haematology guidance).

options.text: Refer for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for him
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with macrocytosis, a low reticulocyte count and dysplastic neutrophils indicates a production failure in the marrow, and aspirate with trephine plus cytogenetics is the only test that separates myelodysplasia from aplastic anaemia and acute leukaemia (Source: Cancer Council Australia haematology guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology).

options.text: Repeat the full blood count in three months before making any referral
options.rationale: Three months of progressive symptoms with a neutrophil count of 1.1 x10^9/L and platelets of 42 x10^9/L carries real infection and bleeding risk that will not be improved by further observation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology).

explanation.summary: Pancytopenia is approached by asking whether the marrow is failing to produce cells or whether cells are being destroyed or sequestered in the periphery, and the reticulocyte count answers that question directly. A low reticulocyte count in the face of significant anaemia indicates failure of production, which narrows the differential to marrow infiltration, aplasia, myelodysplasia and nutritional deficiency. Macrocytosis with dysplastic changes such as hypogranular or hypolobated neutrophils points strongly toward myelodysplastic syndrome, which is a disease of older adults and carries a risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia. Cytogenetics and molecular testing on the marrow sample determine both the prognostic score and the treatment, so referral rather than empirical therapy is the priority.
key_points: The reticulocyte count separates production failure from peripheral destruction
A low count with anaemia indicates the marrow is not responding
Macrocytosis with dysplastic neutrophils suggests myelodysplastic syndrome
Normal B12 and folate exclude megaloblastic causes of macrocytosis
Aspirate with trephine and cytogenetics establishes diagnosis and prognosis
explanation.pearls: Absence of splenomegaly is a useful negative in pancytopenia, because hypersplenism from cirrhosis or a lymphoproliferative disorder produces sequestration with a preserved or raised reticulocyte count rather than the production failure seen here.
